body:
## Overview
Yes. TTLCache.get still returns a value exactly ttl seconds after put. Entries expire only once strictly older than ttl.

## How it works
The decision is one line, `cache.py:20`: `if self.clock() - stored > self.ttl:` in `get` (`cache.py:15-23`). Equal age returns the value; older deletes the entry and returns default. `put` (`cache.py:12-13`) stamps `self.clock()`; the clock is injectable (default `time.monotonic`).

## Why it is this way
Direct (commit 2e2afb8, "Keep cache entries through their last second (#12)", Ana): on coarse clocks (monotonic ticks in ~15 ms steps on some platforms) ttl=1 entries expired on the first read after a one-tick advance. Serving until strictly older than ttl makes ttl the minimum lifetime callers can rely on. The original (d6cba38, Sam) used `>=`. Searched: git log/blame for cache.py (only two commits); no tests, docs or PR text in the repo beyond the commit message.

## Evidence
Fake clock, ttl=10: `9.999 'v'`, `10 'v'`, `10.001 'MISS'`.

## Gotchas
Real lifetime is ttl plus up to the time until the next get; expired entries are only deleted lazily on get. No tests cover the boundary.
